prompt: Billing and analytics both need every payment event. How are they set up?
hint: Where does a message wait until somebody has dealt with it?

choices.text: Two subscriptions on one topic
choices.why: Right: each subscription receives its own copy and keeps its own record of what was acknowledged.

choices.text: One subscription that both services read from
choices.why: Readers sharing a subscription share its messages: each message goes to one of them, so each service would see about half.

choices.text: Two topics, with the app publishing every event to each
choices.why: That works and doubles the publisher's work for nothing; the fan-out is what subscriptions are for.

choices.text: One topic read directly by both, with no subscription
choices.why: A topic keeps nothing for a reader; messages are only ever read from a subscription.

prompt: `analytics` was pulled with `--auto-ack` and came back empty the second time. Why did `billing` still receive the payments?
hint: What does an acknowledgement remove a message from?

choices.text: Billing was pulled first
choices.why: It was pulled second, and the order of the pulls does not matter here.

choices.text: The filter on billing made Pub/Sub keep a separate copy of the payments
choices.why: Every subscription keeps its own copy, filter or not; the filter only decides which messages it is given.

choices.text: An ack removes the message from that subscription and from no other
choices.why: Right: acking in analytics left billing's copies untouched.

choices.text: The emulator ignores acknowledgements
choices.why: It honoured them: the second pull of analytics was empty.

prompt: Billing should receive payments only, and the payment details are inside the JSON body. Why did `events.py` also send `type` as an attribute?
hint: What does Pub/Sub read of a message, and what does it leave alone?

choices.text: Attributes are cheaper than data on the bill
choices.why: The pricing page counts attributes in the size of a message, like the data.

choices.text: A filter reads attributes and never the body
choices.why: Right: Pub/Sub does not parse `data`, so what a filter selects on has to be an attribute.

choices.text: The body is encrypted, so the subscription cannot read it
choices.why: The body is bytes Pub/Sub never parses; encryption has nothing to do with filters.

choices.text: gcloud prints only attributes in its table
choices.why: It prints the data too; the format chosen in the lesson simply left it out.

prompt: A fraud check is added a week after launch, as a new subscription on `app-events`, which has no topic retention. What does it receive on its first pull?
hint: When does a subscription start receiving?

choices.text: The last seven days of events, the default retention
choices.why: Seven days is how long a subscription keeps its own unacked messages; this one has none yet.

choices.text: Only events published after it was created
choices.why: Right: the topic kept nothing for it, so its first pull in the lesson came back empty.

choices.text: Every event the other subscriptions have not acknowledged
choices.why: Their backlogs belong to them; a new subscription does not inherit any of it.

choices.text: An error, because the topic already has subscribers
choices.why: A topic takes any number of subscriptions; the creation succeeded.

prompt: A push endpoint answers `503`. What does Pub/Sub do with the message?
hint: The receiver of the lesson answered 503 twice.

choices.text: Treats it as a nack and sends it again
choices.why: Right: message 17 arrived three times, until a 204 acknowledged it.

choices.text: Moves it to the dead-letter topic at once
choices.why: A dead-letter topic takes a message only after the configured number of attempts, five at least.

choices.text: Drops it, since the endpoint said it was unavailable
choices.why: Dropping on an error would lose messages; any non-2xx answer is a nack.

choices.text: Switches the subscription to pull
choices.why: The kind of subscription changes only when somebody changes its configuration.

prompt: `subscriber.py` received six of the eight new events, and message 10 was missing. Why?
hint: What happened to message 10 just before the program started?

choices.text: The filter removed it
choices.why: `analytics` has no filter; it receives everything.

choices.text: It was lent to the earlier gcloud pull, and its deadline had not run out
choices.why: Right: a pulled message is out of reach until it is acked or its ack deadline expires; it came back in a later section.

choices.text: Streaming pull skips messages that a unary pull has seen
choices.why: No such rule exists; message 10 was delivered later, to the same program.

choices.text: It was acknowledged by the ack command
choices.why: The ack named message 9's ack id only.

prompt: A callback in the Python client spends 40 seconds on one message, on a subscription whose ack deadline is 10 seconds. What happens?
hint: What does the library do while a callback is still running?

choices.text: The message is delivered again after 10 seconds
choices.why: That is what happens to a gcloud pull, which nobody extends; the client library keeps the lease alive.

choices.text: The callback is killed at 10 seconds
choices.why: The library does not interrupt a callback; deadlines are about the message, not the thread.

choices.text: The library extends the deadline while the callback runs
choices.why: Right: by default it keeps extending for up to an hour, so a slow callback does not cause a redelivery and a dead process does.

choices.text: Pub/Sub raises the subscription's ack deadline to 40 seconds
choices.why: The subscription's setting does not change; the library extends the lease on that one message.

prompt: Order status events must keep their order per customer. What should the ordering key be?
hint: The smallest thing whose events must stay in order.

choices.text: The customer id
choices.why: Right: each customer's events keep their order, and customers are free of each other.

choices.text: The store
choices.why: Three stores give three keys, and every customer of a store waits behind every other one.

choices.text: A constant such as `orders`
choices.why: One key is one lane: the whole topic would be ordered and limited to the throughput of a single key.

choices.text: The message id
choices.why: A key unique per message orders nothing, because no two messages share it.

prompt: `redeliver.py` nacked `o-102 placed` on the ordered subscription. On Google, what does the reader receive next for key `c-02`?
hint: What the emulator did is the other half of the lesson's figure.

choices.text: `o-102 packed`, then `o-102 delivered`, then `o-102 placed`
choices.why: That is what the emulator delivered, and it breaks the order the subscription asked for.

choices.text: Only `o-102 packed`; the nacked message goes to the dead-letter topic
choices.why: One nack is one attempt; dead-lettering needs the configured number, five at least.

choices.text: `o-102 placed` again, then `o-102 packed`
choices.why: Right: the service redelivers the nacked message and every later one of its key, in order, even ones already acked.

choices.text: Nothing more for that key until a person intervenes
choices.why: The key resumes with the redelivery; no person is needed.

prompt: Publishing a message with ordering key `c-17` fails after the library's retries. What happens to the next publish with `c-17`?
hint: What would happen to the order if the next message went through?

choices.text: It is sent, and the failed message is retried behind it
choices.why: Then the later message would overtake the earlier one, the exact thing ordering is for.

choices.text: It fails at once, until the program calls `resume_publish` for the key
choices.why: Right: the client pauses the key so that nothing overtakes the message that did not go, and the program decides what to do.

choices.text: It succeeds without an ordering key
choices.why: The library does not strip keys; it pauses the key.

choices.text: Every key of the publisher is paused
choices.why: Only the key whose publish failed is paused; the others go on.

prompt: Why did the billing worker nack the payment `"23,50"` instead of acking it and moving on?
hint: What would an ack have done to the payment?

choices.text: An ack would have lost the payment in silence
choices.why: Right: a nack asks for it again, and the dead-letter topic then keeps it for a person to look at.

choices.text: Nacking is faster than acking
choices.why: Speed is not the point; what each one does to the message is.

choices.text: The emulator refuses acks for messages with errors
choices.why: Pub/Sub never looks inside the data, so it knows nothing of the error.

choices.text: Acks are only allowed after a successful database write
choices.why: Pub/Sub has no idea what the consumer writes; the ordering of work and ack is the consumer's choice.

prompt: What is the smallest maximum number of delivery attempts a dead-letter policy accepts?
hint: `gcloud` refused 3 before sending anything.

prompt: After `seek --time` to ten minutes earlier, `analytics` replayed eleven messages, and none of ids 1 to 9. Why not those?
hint: When were they acknowledged, and what was the subscription keeping then?

choices.text: They were older than ten minutes
choices.why: All of them were published within the last ten minutes of the run; age was not the reason.

choices.text: Seek replays only messages that were never delivered
choices.why: Seek to a time marks retained messages unacknowledged, delivered or not; the eleven had all been delivered.

choices.text: They were acknowledged before `--retain-acked-messages` was turned on, so nothing kept them
choices.why: Right: an acked message is gone from its subscription unless retention of acked messages, or topic retention, keeps it.

choices.text: The filter on billing removed them
choices.why: The filter belongs to billing; analytics was the subscription that was seeked.

prompt: Three subscriptions on `app-events` each need to replay up to a week. Which setting keeps that history most cheaply?
hint: How many copies does each option store?

choices.text: `--retain-acked-messages` with seven days on each subscription
choices.why: That keeps one copy per subscription, three in all, each billed as storage.

choices.text: Topic retention of seven days
choices.why: Right: the topic stores one copy and every attached subscription seeks into it.

choices.text: A snapshot of each subscription every day
choices.why: A snapshot lasts at most seven days and each is billed for what it holds; it suits a planned change, not a rolling week.

choices.text: A longer ack deadline
choices.why: The ack deadline is about one delivery, measured in seconds; it keeps no history.

prompt: A subscription was created with `--min-retry-delay=20s`. After a nack, the emulator delivered the message again in under a second. What does that test say about the retry policy on Google?
hint: Which side of the line between enforced and ignored is this on?

choices.text: The policy is broken and should not be used
choices.why: The emulator ignored it; that says nothing about the service, which documents the wait.

choices.text: It works only for push subscriptions
choices.why: A retry policy applies to pull subscriptions as well; nothing in the run was about push.

choices.text: That it waits about one second
choices.why: The second was the emulator's own speed, not a reading of the policy.

choices.text: Nothing: it was stored and not applied
choices.why: Right: Google documents a wait between the two bounds, and this lab cannot show it.

prompt: A topic receives 1 TiB in a month and has three subscriptions, none filtered. At $40 per TiB and ignoring the free 10 GiB, what is the throughput bill in USD?
hint: Throughput is the publish plus one delivery per subscription.

prompt: Billing receives two events in eight through a filter on `app-events`. What does moving billing to a topic of its own, fed only payments, change on the bill?
hint: How are filtered messages billed?

choices.text: Nothing, since a filter already removes the other events
choices.why: A filter removes them from delivery and not from the bill: Pub/Sub acks them automatically and charges the throughput.

choices.text: It raises the bill, because a second topic is charged per hour
choices.why: Pub/Sub charges no fee per topic; it charges bytes.

choices.text: It removes the delivery charge for the six events in eight billing never wanted
choices.why: Right: about a third of the throughput line in the lesson's arithmetic, at the price of the app publishing payments twice.

choices.text: It removes the 1 KB minimum per request
choices.why: The minimum applies to every request on every topic.

prompt: Match each problem to the Pub/Sub setting that answers it.
hint: One setting keeps history, one moves a message aside, one selects, one orders.

pairs.left: A payment nobody can parse keeps coming back
Billing wants payments and nothing else
A customer's status changes must arrive in order
A bug found on Monday needs the weekend replayed

prompt: Put in order what happened to the payment `"23,50"` in the lesson.
hint: The dead-letter subscription is read last.
items: The billing worker fails to parse it and nacks it
After the fifth attempt, Pub/Sub publishes it to `app-events-dead`
A pull from `billing-dead` shows it with the attributes that say where it came from

prompt: Which of these did the emulator do as Google documents? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate what ran as the service runs from what it accepted and ignored.

choices.text: Forward a message to the dead-letter topic after five attempts
choices.why: Right, with the service's own attribute names.

choices.text: Deliver a nacked ordered message before the later ones of its key
choices.why: It delivered `o-102 packed` first.

choices.text: Retry a push request that got a 503
choices.why: Right, with the same message id each time.

choices.text: Delete a message once its retention had passed
choices.why: The message was still there eleven minutes after a ten-minute retention.

choices.text: Give only the filtered messages to billing
choices.why: Right: billing received ids 4 and 7 and nothing else.

hint: `--auto-ack` sends it for you.
